analysis.one_liner: Hands all fracking regulation to the states, including on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in the Senate Energy Committee until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give each state the only power to regulate hydraulic fracturing — fracking — within its borders, including fracking done on federal land such as national forests: federal agencies would have to follow the state's rules instead of writing their own. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that frack wells, especially on federal land. They would answer to one regulator — the state where they drill — instead of a federal layer of rules that the Interior Department was preparing for fracking on public land.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives states the sole authority to write and enforce any fracking rule, permit requirement, or guidance within their boundaries, and makes fracking on federal land subject only to the law of the state where the land sits.
It would displace federal fracking rules for federal land that the Interior Department announced it intended to write starting in 2011 — a fact the bill's own findings section cites.
Companies drilling on national forests or other public land would face a single state regulator rather than both state and federal permitting.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near fracking on federal land, and the public generally, since national forests and other federal land belong to all Americans. They would lose a federal baseline of oversight and depend entirely on the stringency of whichever state's rules apply.

drawbacks.text: State oil and gas rules vary widely. Under the bill, drilling on land owned by the whole nation would follow the rules of whichever state the land happens to sit in, so a state could permit practices on federal land that federal land managers would not.
The bill removes the federal government's authority over the fracking process itself on federal land, leaving no national backstop if a state's rules are weak.

The honest case for it, which the bill's findings make at length: states have regulated oil and gas drilling for decades, and studies and regulators cited in the bill found no proven case of groundwater contamination from the fracking process itself, so overlapping federal and state rules add permitting delay without proven water-quality benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is administrative: one regulator instead of two, which mainly saves drilling companies compliance cost and time. The cost is structural: federal land is public land, and the bill gives the state where a parcel sits complete say over fracking on it, eliminating any national floor. Because state rules range from strict to minimal, the public's protection would depend on geography rather than a consistent standard. The findings' cited studies address the fracking process itself but not the surface discharges, wastewater disposal, and air emissions the bill acknowledges are separately regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced the bill on March 19, 2015, joined by 26 named Republican cosponsors in the introduction and a total of 28 cosponsors on the bill's record.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; no further action appears in the bill's history.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired in committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal authority over fracking on federal land stayed intact, and drilling companies did not get the state-only rules they sought. People who live near federal-land drilling kept the existing federal layer of oversight that this bill would have removed.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and every cosponsor were Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where party splits could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill would spare fracking companies a second, federal set of rules on public land, overriding the Interior Department's planned federal fracking rule for federal land. The savings come at the expense of a national oversight baseline for water and land the public owns.

industries.industry: Federal land and drilling regulators (Bureau of Land Management and Interior Department)
industries.note: The bill strips these agencies of authority over the fracking process on federal land, precisely where the Interior Department had announced it would write new rules. Their loss is the public's loss of a federal backstop.

The bill makes each state the permanent, sole gatekeeper for fracking within its borders, including on federal land. States with strong rules would protect water well; states with minimal rules would leave the public on federal land in their state with no federal floor.
